stages.title: Define
stages.plain: Write down what you're building in plain English — who it's for, the 3 things it must do, and what you're NOT building.
stages.why: Code is cheap to write and expensive to change. An hour of questions here beats a month of rebuilding. The 'not doing' list is what makes a project finishable.

questions.explain: Force the whole app into one breath. If you can't say it in one sentence, you don't know what it is yet — and neither will anyone else.
questions.example: 'This app lets dog walkers record walks and bill owners without chasing WhatsApp messages.'

questions.ask: Who is the first real user? A named person or a type — not 'everyone'.
questions.explain: Pick one specific person or a tight type you can actually reach and phone. 'Everyone' means no one — you can't build for a crowd you can't picture.
questions.example: 'Sarah — the dog walker on my street. ~15 regular clients, currently invoices by text at month-end.'

questions.ask: What are the 3 things it must do on day one?
questions.explain: Three, not thirty. If the app launched with ONLY these and nothing else, would your first user still use it? If not, the list is wrong.
questions.example: '1) Log a walk with photos. 2) Owner gets a walk summary. 3) Monthly invoice generated automatically.'

questions.ask: What are you deliberately NOT building in version 1?
questions.explain: This list protects you. Every 'wouldn't it be cool if…' goes here, not into the build. Scope creep kills more apps than bad code.
questions.example: 'NOT in v1: live GPS tracking, in-app chat, owner reviews, a marketplace of walkers.'

questions.ask: What does 'launched' mean — the moment you'll call it done?
questions.explain: Pick a concrete, observable moment — not 'when it feels ready'. A vague finish line is why side-projects never finish.
questions.example: 'Launched = Sarah has used it for a full week of real walks and sent one real invoice to a real client.'

stages.gate: You can explain the app to a stranger in 30 seconds, and the not-doing list makes you slightly uncomfortable.

traps.trap: Building before defining — the not-doing list gets skipped
traps.story: Real example: the CRM this app grew out of had its balance system rewritten three times because 'what counts as paid' was never written down first. An hour of Stage 0 would have saved a month.

traps.trap: Answering 'everyone' for the first user
traps.story: If your app is 'for everyone' it's for no one. The first user should be a person you could phone. 'Novices building apps' only worked once we named the actual person: you.

traps.trap: Scope creep disguised as planning
traps.story: Happened live in this build: mid-Stage-0, 'let's add bots' appeared — a real feature, but the right move was writing it down, deciding deliberately, THEN building. Ideas arriving mid-build is normal; letting them jump the queue is how projects die.

stages.title: Architect
stages.plain: Decide only the things that are expensive to change later: who can see whose data, where secrets live, what it talks to.
stages.why: Get these wrong and you pay forever; get them right and everything else is fast and loose.

questions.ask: Can user A ever see user B's data? What's the worst that happens if they do?
questions.explain: Every record should belong to someone, and every database query should filter by owner. The worst-case answer decides how careful you must be.
questions.example: 'Worst case: one walker sees another's client addresses + prices — bad. So every record carries a user_id and the API filters on it, always.'

questions.ask: What changes per user/deployment? That belongs in the database, never in code.
questions.explain: Anything that varies between your laptop, the live server, or different customers belongs in config (env vars or the database) — never hardcoded.
questions.example: 'Database URL, email sender address, the app name — all env vars. The code stays identical everywhere it runs.'

questions.ask: What keys/passwords does it need? They live in env vars — never the repo.
questions.explain: List every secret the app needs. They live in environment variables on the server — the moment one lands in code or git, assume it's stolen.
questions.example: 'AI_API_KEY, RESEND_API_KEY, MONGO_URL, JWT_SECRET — all in Render env vars, none in the repo.'

questions.ask: What does it talk to (payments, email, AI)? What's the fallback if it's down?
questions.explain: Email providers, payment systems and AI APIs all go down sometimes. Decide now what the app does when each fails — degraded beats dead.
questions.example: 'AI provider down → mentor serves the written stage guide for free. Email down → admin hands out the reset link manually.'

questions.ask: Name the 5–10 core 'things' (e.g. user, project, payment) and how they relate.
questions.explain: The nouns and how they relate — 'a user has many projects'. If you can't draw it in five boxes, your AI builder will invent something worse.
questions.example: 'User → many Projects. Project → 8 Stage records → answers + mentor messages. CreditTransaction → belongs to User.'

stages.gate: Every decision is written down WITH its reasoning — and the 'if wrong, how bad?' answers are all small.

traps.trap: Copying architecture from a tutorial or a bigger app
traps.story: The CRM needed a separate database per customer — it stores children's data. This app uses one shared DB with user_id tags — it stores project checklists. Same builder, opposite answers. Isolation is a per-app decision driven by data sensitivity, not a religion.

traps.trap: Secrets ending up in code 'temporarily'
traps.story: API keys pasted into source get scraped by bots within minutes of pushing to GitHub — this is automated, not hypothetical. 'I'll move it to env vars later' is how keys leak. Env vars from line one, always.

traps.trap: Bolting auth on later
traps.story: Retrofitting 'who is this user?' to a single-user app means touching every screen and every query. Adding it day one costs an afternoon; adding it in month three costs a rewrite.

stages.title: Foundation
stages.plain: The boring plumbing: repo on GitHub, database, a blank page live on a real URL — before any features.
stages.why: Deploying 'hello world' on day one flushes out every environment problem while the stakes are zero.
guided_steps: Create the GitHub repo: gh auth login (once) → gh repo create <name> --private --source=. --push — run inside the project folder
Deploy on Render: Dashboard → New → Blueprint → pick your repo → it reads render.yaml and fills in build/start commands
Set env vars in Render → Environment: MONGO_URL (database connection string — change the db name at the end to your app's name)
Click Deploy → wait ~3 min → open your URL and check it loads
Verify the pipeline: push any small change to main and watch it redeploy by itself
stages.gate: Push to main → live URL updates → page loads. You could break it right now and recover in under 5 minutes (revert the commit).
checklist: GitHub repo created and code pushed to main
Render web service created (Blueprint or manual)
MONGO_URL set in Render Environment — database connected
Live URL loads the page
Pushed a small change and watched it auto-deploy

traps.trap: Forgetting the env var — the app deploys but the database is silent
traps.story: Happened verbatim in this build: AppPilot deployed fine, health check said db: 'not_configured' — because MONGO_URL was never set. Deployment succeeding doesn't mean it's working; always check the health endpoint, not just 'did it deploy'.

traps.trap: Building features before the pipeline exists
traps.story: The tempting order is: build it all locally, deploy at the end. What actually happens: three weeks of code meets hosting config that doesn't work, and you're debugging a dozen problems at once. Blank page live on day one flushes every plumbing issue while stakes are zero.

traps.trap: Manual deploy steps you have to remember
traps.story: If deploying means 'run these 5 commands in the right order', you WILL eventually skip one and deploy a broken build. Auto-deploy-on-push means the pipeline can't be forgotten — the repo IS the deploy button.

stages.title: First Slice
stages.plain: ONE real feature end to end — a user clicks something and real data moves through the whole system.
stages.why: A slice is demonstrable — you can click it and know it works. Layers give you 80% of nothing; a slice gives you 100% of something.
stages.gate: A stranger could perform the action without you explaining anything — and you've watched it work, not just believed it works.
checklist: Picked the single most valuable action a user can take
Built just enough UI → API → database for that one action
Verified it end-to-end with real-ish data
A stranger could do it without you explaining

traps.trap: Building in layers instead of slices
traps.story: 'First the database, then all the API, then the UI' produces 80% of nothing for weeks. AppPilot's first slice was signup→create project→save answers — ugly but real. You could click it, break it, show someone. That's a slice.

traps.trap: Trusting 'it looks right' over actually testing
traps.story: The gate check that blocked Stage 1 before Stage 0 was complete? That was caught by curl-ing the API, not by eyeballing code. Verified beats believed — every time you think 'obviously works', test it and be surprised occasionally.

stages.title: Feature Slices
stages.plain: The rest of the must-do features — one thin slice at a time, each deployed and verified before the next starts.
stages.why: Each slice is small enough to revert in seconds and complete enough to show a user.
stages.gate: Every must-do from Stage 0 works on the live URL — and nothing from the not-doing list snuck in.
checklist: Every must-do item from Stage 0 works on the live URL
Each slice was deployed and verified before starting the next
Nothing from the not-doing list snuck in

traps.trap: Gates that auto-pass — decoration instead of enforcement
traps.story: Real bug found in this build: stages with no questions auto-passed because 'nothing missing' meant 'complete'. A gate that can't fail isn't a gate. Check your gates actually BLOCK something — try to sneak past them.

traps.trap: Charging before success
traps.story: Found in this build too: mentor credits were deducted BEFORE the AI call — an API outage would have charged users for a canned fallback. Billing/metering bugs are invisible until someone audits them. Charge after success, always.

traps.trap: Unrelated fix sneaking into a change
traps.story: While lightening the chat sidebar in the CRM, the global admin sidebar accidentally went light too — a CSS variable shared across pages. The fix: revert, scope the change tighter. Small commits make this a 2-minute undo instead of archaeology.

stages.title: Harden
stages.plain: Make it safe for strangers: permissions, validation, backups, secrets audit, error handling.
stages.why: Too early = hardening features that get rewritten. Too late = real users hit real holes. Right moment: after features work, before strangers arrive.
guided_steps: Secrets sweep: run `git log -p | grep -i -E 'api_key|secret|password|mongodb\+srv'` — if anything real shows up, rotate that key immediately (assume it's leaked)
Check .gitignore covers .env files, then check `git ls-files | grep env` returns nothing
Isolation test: create a second account, copy its data ID, try to open it while logged in as the first user — must fail with 404/403, not work
Abuse test: signups and any paid-per-use feature (AI calls, emails) need rate limits or credits — assume someone will script it
Input test: paste emoji, 10,000 characters, and `<script>alert(1)</script>` into every form — nothing should crash or execute
Passwords: stored hashed (bcrypt/argon2/salted SHA), never plaintext, never logged
HTTPS: your host must serve HTTPS only — check the padlock, check http:// redirects
Backup: do a restore to a scratch database and open the data — an untested backup is a wish, not a backup
Dependencies: `npm audit` / `pip-audit` — fix anything marked critical before launch
Errors: make sure a crash logs somewhere you check (Render logs, Sentry) — silent failures are how breaches go unnoticed for months

questions.ask: If your database leaked tomorrow, what's the worst thing in it? Does that change what you're storing?
questions.explain: The answer changes what you choose to store. If the worst item is unforgivable, stop storing it — you can't leak what you never kept.
questions.example: 'Emails + hashed passwords — embarrassing, not catastrophic. No card numbers, no kids' addresses. Payment data lives at Stripe, not with me.'

questions.ask: Who would bother attacking your app — bored script-kiddie, competitor, someone wanting free AI credits?
questions.explain: You're not fighting nation-states. Know your real attacker: script-kiddies scanning for easy wins, or freeloaders wanting your paid features free.
questions.example: 'Most likely: someone farming free mentor chats with throwaway accounts — that's why credit limits and email verification exist.'

questions.ask: What can a stranger do for free that costs YOU money? How is it capped?
questions.explain: Every free action that calls a paid API is a hole in your wallet. Find them all, cap them all — rate limits and credits are how.
questions.example: 'Mentor messages cost me real money per call → capped by credits. Reset emails → capped by rate limiting.'

questions.ask: If you discovered user data was accessed last week, what's your first three moves?
questions.explain: Panic is the default response. Write your first three moves now while you're calm — contain, assess, tell.
questions.example: '1) Rotate all keys + kill all sessions. 2) Work out whose data was touched. 3) Email affected users honestly — same day.'

stages.gate: You tried to break it as an attacker and couldn't — and you could lose the database right now and recover.
checklist: Tried to reach another user's data while logged in as someone else — failed
Secrets audit: no keys/passwords anywhere in git history (checked with git log -p)
Backup exists AND a restore was actually tested
Bad input doesn't crash it — forms reject garbage safely
Errors are logged somewhere you'll actually look
Anything that costs money per use (AI, email, SMS) is rate-limited or credit-gated
Passwords hashed at rest; sessions can be revoked; HTTPS only
npm audit / pip-audit run — no critical vulnerabilities unfixed
Every security question above has a written answer

traps.trap: Emailing real users from a test system
traps.story: In the CRM, a test run nearly emailed real parents about fake payments. That's why the email sandbox exists — outbound mail is blocked by default anywhere that isn't production, and every send is logged. If your app sends messages, build the off-switch before you need it.

traps.trap: Hiding data in the UI instead of blocking it in the API
traps.story: Showing a lock icon in React while the API happily serves the data is security theatre. Verified in this build: another user's project returns 404 — not 'hidden', nonexistent to you. Curious users open dev tools; enforce at the API.

traps.trap: A backup that's never been restored
traps.story: Backups fail silently for months — wrong flags, missing permissions, corrupted files — and you find out the day you need them. An untested backup is a wish, not a backup. Restore to a scratch database once, for real.

stages.title: Launch
stages.plain: One friendly human uses it for its real purpose — watch where they hesitate. Then open wider.
stages.why: Every assumption gets tested in the first 10 minutes of a real person clicking around. Better they're forgiving.
stages.gate: A real person completed the core action without your help — and nothing in Harden got skipped 'just for launch'.
checklist: One named human used it for its real purpose
Watched or recorded where they hesitated
Fixed the top confusion points
Nothing from Harden was skipped 'just for launch'

traps.trap: Launching to everyone at once
traps.story: A big launch multiplies every undiscovered bug by every user. One friendly human first — you watch them click, they forgive the rough edges, and their confusion is your fix list. Widen only when they sail through.

traps.trap: Skipping Harden 'just for launch' — and never coming back
traps.story: 'We'll add rate limits after launch' is how real users discover the hole. Harden exists precisely because post-launch you never go back — you're too busy with launch problems. Gate 6 exists to catch this exact sentence.

traps.trap: No disclaimers or legal pages until someone complains
traps.story: Even free beta products need: privacy (you hold emails), terms (AI can be wrong — say so), a support path. It takes an afternoon, not a lawyer — but pretending you don't need it is the trap.

stages.title: Operate
stages.plain: The app tells you what's wrong before users do — health checks, logs, error alerts — then the loop repeats: define next slice → build → deploy → observe.
stages.why: Software is never finished, it's maintained. Winners notice problems fastest and fix them smallest.
stages.gate: Never ends — this stage IS the product.
checklist: Health/status check exists and you've looked at it
Errors land somewhere you check
Users have a feedback path (even an email link)
You've run the loop once: observe → next slice → deploy

traps.trap: Silent failures — errors that vanish
traps.story: In this build the AI mentor was failing silently and serving fallback text — users would never know the difference, and neither would we. The fix was logging the error to Render's logs. If a failure produces no signal, it doesn't exist — until a user notices.

traps.trap: Finding out from users instead of your own checks
traps.story: The health endpoint shows which commit is deployed and whether the database is connected — one curl answers 'is it alive and is it the right version?' in a second. If the first sign of trouble is a user's email, you're operating blind.
